content: Provider-assisted referral should be offered to men diagnosed with sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or viral hepatitis, as well as to men whose partners are living with HIV. Social network-based HIV testing approaches may be considered for men from key populations, provided these methods are feasible and supported by national policies. Secondary distribution of HIV self-testing (HIVST) kits by antenatal care (ANC) women to their male partners, and by peers from key populations to their partners and social contacts, has proven effective in increasing HIV testing services (HTS) uptake among men. Community-based HTS is particularly important for reaching men, as they are often less likely than women to utilize health facilities. These community-based approaches are especially useful for men who have never been tested or those from key populations, including men with partners from these groups. Focused community and peer mobilization, as well as mobile outreach with HIVST distribution, can facilitate testing among men. In southern Africa, combination prevention trials have demonstrated the benefits of widespread implementation of community-based HTS, particularly home-based testing, followed by rapid antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation. Sustained home-based testing has increased treatment coverage, reduced mortality, and, as shown in a Zambian study, decreased HIV incidence. In high HIV burden settings, such as southern Africa, mobile outreach during evenings or weekends, community-delivered HIVST (by partners or providers), and provider-assisted referral have been effective in reaching men. Across all community-based HTS approaches, programs must carefully consider and implement methods to ensure linkage to care. Without proper linkage, men diagnosed with HIV may not benefit from early ART initiation. Workplaces can also serve as important venues for reaching men. HIV testing initiatives in workplaces have identified many previously undiagnosed infections. For example, in a mining company in South Africa, 2,257 employees collected 3,202 HIVST kits, with 42% of those collecting kits having never been tested or not tested in the preceding 12 months. Among those who reported their results, 16% were HIV-positive. Workplace HTS should be implemented within a framework of policies that protect workers who test HIV-positive from job loss and discrimination. Lay provider-delivered HTS should be considered across all approaches targeting men, as it can facilitate HTS uptake, provider-assisted referral, and affordability. While scaling up HTS approaches for men has many benefits, it can be costly, necessitating efforts to optimize resource use and efficiency. Adolescents and young people, particularly those aged 10–24 years, remain highly vulnerable to HIV acquisition due to social and contextual factors such as age, gender, cultural norms, economic and educational status, and sexual orientation. Despite their vulnerability, adolescents are less likely to be tested than adults, leaving many undiagnosed and untreated. Adolescents and young people may benefit from HTS as part of broader HIV prevention and sexual and reproductive health interventions. HTS should be prioritized for perinatally HIV-infected individuals who were not diagnosed in infancy, adolescents from key populations, and vulnerable groups such as street children, orphans, and those in child-headed households. HTS for adolescents should be adolescent-friendly, addressing their psychological and physical health needs in a non-judgmental, non-discriminatory, and confidential manner. Referral and linkage pathways to HIV prevention, treatment, and care are crucial, as is linkage to other adolescent-specific services, including sexual and reproductive health services. Social media and web-based approaches, developed in consultation with youth groups, may reduce barriers to accessing HTS and other services. HIV self-testing has been shown to be effective and acceptable among adolescents and young people, doubling HTS uptake compared to standard facility-based testing. Adolescents who test HIV-positive may require additional support with disclosure and emotional support. Providers should engage trusted adults, with the adolescent’s consent, to support them in managing living with HIV. Risk-based screening tools may be considered to identify adolescents in need of HTS, but tools designed to exclude individuals from testing may not be appropriate in high HIV burden settings. WHO recommends that adolescents themselves be involved in the decision to accept HTS. Governments should review and revise age of consent policies to recognize adolescents’ rights to make choices about their health. HTS providers should be aware of country laws governing the age of consent and ensure that children and adolescents have access to HTS.
